title: India's Quiet Kitchen Takeover: Seven Indian-Chef-Led Restaurants Crack Asia's 50 Best Extended List
excerpt: From Mumbai's Papa's to Bangkok's Gaa, Indian culinary talent is showing up across Asia's most prestigious restaurant rankings — and the diaspora is eating well.
body:
When the Asia's 50 Best Restaurants 2026 list was announced in Hong Kong in March, India secured two coveted spots in the main top-50 ranking: Masque in Mumbai at No. 15 — crowned the best restaurant in India for an unprecedented fifth consecutive year — and Naar, a destination restaurant nestled deep in the Indian Himalayas, at No. 30. But the story that went underreported was what happened in the extended 51-100 list, where seven restaurants led by Indian chefs staked their claim, four of them in India and three abroad.

The showing was selected by more than 350 culinary experts spanning 27 cities across Asia. Together, it amounts to a quiet but unmistakable statement: Indian chefs are no longer an emerging force in Asia's fine-dining landscape. They have arrived.

## The Restaurants

In Mumbai, Papa's ranked No. 66. Chef Hussain Shahzad runs a 12-seater counter offering an unconventional tasting menu that reimagines familiar Indian flavours — think mawa khaja transformed into a cronut filled with burnt honey custard and brunost, a Norwegian brown cheese. Also in Mumbai, The Table ranked No. 73, serving sharing plates that draw from cuisines across Asia, Europe, and the Americas.

In New Delhi, Inja secured No. 75. Chef Adwait Anantwar's menu is a striking Indian-Japanese dialogue — shiso leaf tuna with pomelo chaat, lobster rasam chawanmushi — that would feel at home in neither Tokyo nor Delhi alone.

Bengaluru's Farmlore, at No. 83, is a different proposition entirely. Founded by chef Johnson Ebenezer and Kaushik Raju, the 18-seat restaurant sits on a working farm, its menu built around whatever the surrounding soil produces that season. It represents a growing farm-to-table movement in Indian fine dining that marries sustainability with regional flavour.

## Indian Chefs Abroad

The list also highlighted Indian culinary talent cooking outside India. In Singapore, Thevar (No. 58) is run by chef Mano Thevar, who draws on his Penang roots and Indian heritage for a modern tasting menu. In Bangkok, chef Garima Arora's Gaa (No. 95) has become one of the most closely watched restaurants in Southeast Asia, blending Indian and Thai traditions with seasonal ingredients. Also in Bangkok, Haoma by chef Deepanker Khosla (No. 96) is celebrated for its zero-waste, farm-to-table philosophy.

Arora, notably, was the first Indian woman to earn a Michelin star — at her previous restaurant, Gaa's predecessor. Her presence on the list, alongside Khosla and Thevar, underscores a pattern: Indian chefs are not just succeeding within the subcontinent's own fine-dining ecosystem. They are shaping culinary conversations from Singapore to Bangkok to Dubai.

## Masque: The Standard-Bearer

At the top of the Indian contingent sits Masque, where chef Varun Totlani has built a ten-course seasonal degustation menu around India's extraordinary wealth of ingredients — Goan seaweed, Kashmiri chilli, sunchoke with ghassi, smoked pork with poha. Masque also won the Art of Hospitality Award, recognising the leadership of entrepreneurial couple Aditi and Aditya Dugar.

Totlani, who started as a commis chef when Masque opened in 2016 and trained at the Culinary Institute of America in New York, represents a generational shift. He is not importing Western techniques to India; he is using global training to excavate the depth already present in Indian ingredients and traditions.

In June, Masque staged a pop-up collaboration at Bangkok's Siam Kempinski Hotel — an eight-course menu featuring squid, sea buckthorn, clams, and Thai wagyu — demonstrating the kind of cross-border culinary diplomacy that was once reserved for French and Japanese kitchens.

## The Diaspora Connection

For NRIs, the list carries a double significance. It validates what the diaspora has long argued — that Indian food, in the right hands, stands alongside any cuisine in the world. And it offers a practical travel itinerary: Mumbai, Delhi, Bengaluru, Singapore, Bangkok, each with an Indian-led restaurant worth crossing borders for.

The full main list of Asia's 50 Best Restaurants 2026 also featured Naar at No. 30, led by chef Prateek Sadhu in the Himalayas — a reminder that India's culinary talent is not concentrated in its metros alone.

As Indian fine dining moves from a handful of trailblazers to a generation-deep bench of talent, the question is no longer whether Indian chefs can compete at the highest level. It is how many tables the world is willing to set for them.
